title.analysis: Authentic title "How Much House Your Salary Actually Buys You" is a personalised, calculable question: "your salary" plus "actually" implies a gap from what lenders say. The transcript delivers this with an itemised payment stack and bank-versus-comfortable income thresholds. Among the five nearest peers (psychology, crypto trap, $50K saved, 0.1 Bitcoin, $50K a year) only this one targets a near-universal life purchase. Its 7.75752 ratio is the cohort high. Association only; no CTR or experiment evidence.

script.opening_words: You're making $80,000 a year. Decent salary, right? You've been responsible. You've saved some money. You're ready to become a homeowner. So, you open Zillow at midnight on a Tuesday and every single house that doesn't look like it's actively falling apart costs at least $400,000. The kitchen has laminate countertops from 2003. The carpet is that specific shade of beige that screams, "We stopped caring in 1997." There's fake wood paneling in the basement and the
script.ending_words: that it doesn't make sense. Not right now. Not at these prices. Not with your current income. And that's not failure. That's math. That's reality. That's making a decision based on what will actually make your life better instead of what everyone else thinks you should do. Your salary buys you a lot less house than you think it does. And understanding that might be the most valuable financial lesson you learn.
script.analysis: Full 18767 canonical characters read. A calculation-led affordability exposé. The relatable Zillow-at-midnight cold open leads to an industry-incentive accusation, then median income versus price, the 28% versus 43% rule, an itemised $400K cost stack, house-poor and comfortable household vignettes, metro contrasts, a generational comparison, hidden costs, other debts, down-payment math, a no-crash forecast, rent versus buy, four options and a permission-giving close. The strongest arithmetic reproduces: the $3,508 stack, $150K/$98K income thresholds, the $250 to $41K capacity rule, the down-payment years and the Texas tax. Errors: the $3,191 scenario contradicts its own itemisation; the $120K DTI is 9.32%, not over 11%; car payment $748 versus $532; P&I $2,179, not $2,150; 21% first-time buyers and age 40 survey medians framed as the average American. Census median income is verified. Most market statistics are unsourced and date-bound.
beat_map: Cold open: $80K earner, Zillow at midnight, $400K fixer-uppers, everyone says approved.
Thesis: you cannot really afford it and nobody in the sale is incentivised to say so; disclaimer.
28% rule versus 43% DTI; bank approval is not affordability.
Itemised $400K example: P&I, tax, insurance, PMI, maintenance = $3,508; $150K versus $98K income.
Only about 20% earn $150K+; typical home unaffordable to typical household.
Metro contrasts: SF, LA, Austin, Atlanta, Cleveland; San Jose versus Cleveland income required.
Parents' era: 3x versus 5x price/income, 1980s rates, college and car costs, boomer and first-time buyer stats.
Hidden costs: maintenance cycles, insurance surge, property taxes.
Other debts and DTI erosion; down-payment saving timeline.
Market outlook: forecasts, lock-in, inventory, rent cheaper than buying.
Options: move, buy less, house hack, wait; permission-giving close.

topic.analysis: US housing affordability: lender qualification versus sustainable budget, full ownership cost stack, regional dispersion, generational price-to-income shift, rate lock-in and rent-versus-buy, ending in practical alternatives.
topic.audience_problem: Prospective first-time buyers approved by lenders who sense they cannot afford homes and want a concrete income-to-price answer and permission to wait.
topic.time_sensitivity: High: the rate (6.09% February 2026), prices, insurance, inventory and forecasts are date-bound; the cost-stack method is evergreen.
topic.narrative_angle: Bank says yes, math says no: itemised calculator plus generational grievance and permission-giving close.
topic.novelty_and_corpus_angle: Build an original affordability calculator video: one transparent itemised cost stack (P&I at a dated rate, tax, insurance, PMI, maintenance) recomputed live for several incomes and metros, every input dated and sourced, and each scenario reconciled so totals match their components.
topic.competition: Same-channel nearest-age peers in K01; not an independent niche or causal test

Errors in several figures did not prevent reach, so source correctness and reach are separate.
